name: Partitioning

origin.note: The fixed-point version ($k$-EPF) was posed with $k$-circle formation in 2021; the earlier partitioning of Efrima and Peleg fixes the number of groups instead and is recorded under $k$-grouping.

derived_from.relation: A partition into groups of size $k$ at points is a pattern of $n/k$ points, each of multiplicity $k$.

related.relation: Partitioning fixes the size of each group; $k$-grouping fixes the number of groups. They coincide for equal-sized groups [Efrima2009Partition].

summary: Robots must partition themselves into distinct groups of exactly $k$ robots each, each group at its own point.
statement: $n$ robots, with $k$ dividing $n$, must partition themselves into $n/k$ groups of exactly $k$ robots, each group gathered at its own point, and stay there. The group size $k$ is given; the number of groups follows from it.

primer.intro: Picture robot cars that must park in groups of exactly $k$ at a few marked charging stations. There are $n$ robots, points in the plane, and $n/k$ **fixed points** that every robot can see; $k$ divides $n$. Each robot repeats a **Look-Compute-Move cycle**: it takes a snapshot of where the other robots are (Look), decides on a destination point (Compute) and moves towards it (Move). Robots are identical, silent and **oblivious** (no memory between cycles); in the basic version they agree on the direction of one axis (say north), all robots see everything, and the scheduler is ASYNC (each phase may take any finite time). The robots must end with exactly $k$ robots on each fixed point, and stay there. The question is for which starting configurations and values of $k$ this is possible.

ideas.title: The easy extreme: one station for everybody
ideas.idea:
A standard approach for the simplest case, $k = n$, where there is only one fixed point:

1. Look for the fixed point.
2. Move straight towards it.
3. Once on it, stay.
ideas.analysis: No coordination is needed, because the fixed point is a landmark all robots recognise: every move either reaches the point or covers at least a minimum distance, so each robot arrives after finitely many cycles. With more than one fixed point the robots must agree who goes where, and robots that look alike may be unable to choose differently; Bhagat, Das, Chakraborty and Mukhopadhyaya characterise the configurations and values of $k$ for which the problem is solvable with one common axis [Bhagat2021kCircle], the catalogue's introductory and current best result (not described in detail here). The opposite extreme, $k = 1$, asks for one robot per fixed point.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows the role of fixed points: they are landmarks that break much of the symmetry robots cannot break themselves.

ideas.title: Mirror twins arrive in pairs
ideas.idea: A standard symmetry argument, for robots that cannot tell left from right. Let $n = 6$ and $k = 3$, and put both fixed points on a vertical line $L$. Place three robots left of $L$ and their three mirror images to the right, none on $L$. Give each pair of mirror twins mirror-image coordinate systems and always wake them together. Twins see mirror-image snapshots, so they make mirror-image moves and stay mirror images forever. A robot can reach a point of $L$ only together with its twin, so every point of $L$ always holds an even number of robots. It can never hold exactly 3.
ideas.analysis: The same parity argument rules out every odd $k$ whenever all fixed points lie on a line of symmetry of the start that holds no robot. This is why the catalogue's setting assumes a common axis, and why the answer depends on the start; the exact characterisation is in [Bhagat2021kCircle].
ideas.why_it_matters: It is a compact example of how symmetry and counting combine to make a placement task impossible.

history: Partitioning into groups of a **given size** was first studied with the group locations fixed in advance ($k$-EPF), together with $k$-circle formation; the question was **for which configurations and values of $k$ it is solvable** when robots share only one axis [Bhagat2021kCircle].

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or epochs (ASYNC) until the task is done; "finite" when only solvability is known

measures.name: Colours
measures.description: colours of the light per robot (0 for oblivious robots)

variants.title: Exactly $k$ robots at each fixed point
variants.summary: With one common axis, the configurations and values of $k$ for which exactly $k$ robots can gather at each of given fixed points are characterised.

results.note: Introductory and current best. Also $k$-circle formation: disjoint circles of $k$ robots each, centred at the fixed points.

open: Partitioning into groups of size $k$ at points chosen by the robots (no fixed points given).
variants.notes: The $k$-EPF problem generalises embedded pattern formation: the fixed points are visible to all robots and each must end with exactly $k$ robots [Bhagat2021kCircle].

figure.caption: Partitioning ($k$-EPF): $n$ robots, $k$ dividing $n$, must gather in groups of exactly $k$ robots at the $n/k$ given fixed points, each point receiving one group [Bhagat2021kCircle]. Shown: the simplest case $k = n$, one fixed point (dashed square), in SSYNC rounds; ringed robots are activated and move straight towards the point, a move possibly stopping early, until all are on it.
